591.quote_or_event: “Four things of paramount value are difficult to obtain here by a living being: human birth, instruction in the Law, belief in it, and energy in self-control.”
591.explanation: Mahavira names energy or exertion (vīrya) in self-control as one of the four rarest and most valuable possessions; verse 10 adds that many who approve of the religion never fulfil it strenuously.
591.tie_back: The Kural says energy is the only thing that truly makes one an owner; the Uttaradhyayana likewise ranks energy among the few possessions of real worth.
591.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 3.1 (cf. 3.10) (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
591._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. Strong fit on energy as a supreme possession; the Jain energy is directed to self-restraint and liberation rather than worldly undertakings.

592.quote_or_event: “Wealth will not protect a careless man in this world and the next. Though he had seen the right way, he does not see it, even as one in the dark whose lamp has suddenly been put out.”
592.explanation: The lecture on carelessness opens by urging exertion and warns that wealth gives no lasting protection to one who lacks vigilance.
592.tie_back: Like the Kural's contrast between energy, which endures, and wealth, which slips away, this verse sets the unreliability of riches against the inner alertness that alone keeps a person on the right road.
592.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 4.5 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
592._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. Good fit on wealth's impermanence versus inner quality; Jacobi's 'careless' (pramāda) is the opposite of Jain exertion, though not identical to the Kural's ookkam.

593.quote_or_event: “Happy are we, happy live we who call nothing our own; when Mithilâ is on fire, nothing is burned that belongs to me.”
593.explanation: When Indra tells the renouncing King Nami that his city and palace are burning, Nami answers that he grieves at nothing because he no longer claims any of it as his own.
593.tie_back: The Kural says those who hold energy firmly do not grieve over lost wealth; Nami likewise does not lament the loss of his kingdom, though his calm rests on non-possession rather than on confidence that energy will win wealth back.
593.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 9.14 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
593._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com (diacritics simplified). The 'no grief at loss' outcome matches; the ground differs, Jain detachment rather than energetic self-reliance.

594.quote_or_event: “Fields and houses, gold, cattle, slaves and servants: where these four goods, the causes of pleasure, are present, in such families he is born. He will have friends and relations, be of good family, of fine complexion, healthy, wise, noble, famous, and powerful.”
594.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana says that one who strenuously fulfils the Law and leaves this body rises to heaven and is later reborn into a family where prosperity and every advantage are already present.
594.tie_back: The Kural pictures prosperity finding its own way to the door of the steadfast; here too prosperity arrives unsought for the one who has striven, though in Jainism it comes through karmic merit and rebirth.
594.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 3.17–18 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
594._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. The 'prosperity comes to the striver' pattern matches loosely; the mechanism is karmic merit across births, and Jainism treats such prosperity as secondary to liberation.

595.quote_or_event: “The pious obtain purity, and the pure stand firmly in the Law: (the soul afterwards) reaches the highest Nirvâna, being like unto a fire fed with ghee.”
595.explanation: After saying that one must fulfil the Law strenuously, the text compares the purified soul to a fire that blazes higher as ghee is poured on it.
595.tie_back: The Kural's flower-stalk rises as high as the water is deep, and a person as high as his energy; the Jain image likewise ties the height the soul reaches to how fully it is fed by effort and purity.
595.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 3.11–12 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
595._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com (diacritics simplified). Both use a natural image of growth proportional to what sustains it, but the Jain simile is about purity leading to nirvana, not the proportion between energy and worldly eminence.

596.quote_or_event: “You have crossed the great ocean; why do you halt so near the shore? make haste to get on the other side; Gautama, be careful all the while!”
596.explanation: Mahavira urges his chief disciple Gautama not to settle for what he has achieved but to press on to the highest goal without a moment's slackness.
596.tie_back: The Kural tells us to let every thought be of rising higher; Mahavira's charge to Gautama is the same refusal to rest short of the highest aim.
596.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 10.34 (refrain from 10.1) (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
596._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com; the closing refrain is given in full in 10.1 and abbreviated '&c.' in 10.34. Good fit on aiming high; the Kural's second line about fate has no Jain counterpart, as Jainism rejects fate in favour of karma and effort.

597.quote_or_event: “As an elephant at the head of the battle, so was Mahâvîra there victorious. … As a hero at the head of the battle is surrounded on all sides, so was there Mahâvîra. Bearing all hardships, the Venerable One, undisturbed, proceeded (on the road to Nirvâna).”
597.explanation: Describing Mahavira's harsh wanderings in Lāḍha, where he was beaten, cut and set upon by dogs, the Acaranga compares him to a war elephant at the front of battle who stays unshaken.
597.tie_back: This is almost the Kural's own image: the strong-minded do not falter in ruin, just as a war elephant pierced by arrows stands firm.
597.source: Ācārāṅga Sūtra 1.8.3.8 and 1.8.3.13 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884; sacred-texts.com)
597._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com (diacritics simplified; ellipsis joins verses 8 and 13). Near one-to-one on the war-elephant image of steadfastness; Mahavira's victory is nonviolent endurance, not military.

598.quote_or_event: “He gave up his gold and silver, his troops and chariots, and distributed, portioned out, and gave away his valuable treasures (consisting of) riches, corn, gold, pearls, &c., and distributed among those who wanted to make presents to others. Thus he gave away during a whole year.”
598.explanation: Before renouncing the world Mahavira spent a whole year giving away his wealth, a great gift that Jain tradition says every Tirthankara makes before renunciation.
598.tie_back: The Kural says only those with energy of spirit can know the joy of being the world's generous givers; in Jainism the year of giving comes from the same resolute spirit that leads to renunciation.
598.source: Ācārāṅga Sūtra 2.15.17 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884; wisdomlib.org)
598._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi's translation on wisdomlib.org. Shows great generosity flowing from inner resolve, but the Jain text does not explicitly tie giving to energy, and the gift is a prelude to renunciation rather than a source of pride, which Jainism counts as a passion.

599.quote_or_event: “As a strong and irresistible elephant of sixty years, surrounded by his females, (has no equal), neither has a very learned monk. … As a proud lion with sharp fangs, who brooks no assault, is superior to all animals, so is a very learned monk (superior to all men).”
599.explanation: In a chain of similes the Uttaradhyayana praises the accomplished monk through the mightiest animals, setting the lion that brooks no assault above all other beasts.
599.tie_back: The Kural's point is that the great elephant still fears the attacking tiger, so courage outweighs size; the Jain verses use the same animal world of strength, with the fearless big cat at the top.
599.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 11.18 and 11.20 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
599._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. Shared animal imagery, but the Jain text praises both elephant and lion and does not set them against each other; the Kural's moral that spirit beats bulk is only implied.

600.quote_or_event: “When the soul has once got into a vegetable-body, it remains long in that state, for an endless time, after which its lot is not much bettered; Gautama, be careful all the while!”
600.explanation: Jain doctrine treats plants as living souls with a single sense; Mahavira warns that a soul which falls into plant-existence through carelessness may stay there for endless time, which is why human birth must not be wasted.
600.tie_back: The Kural says people without inner energy are mere trees in human form; Jainism makes the warning literal, since slackness can lead the soul into an actual vegetable body.
600.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 10.9 (refrain from 10.1) (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
600._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com; 10.9 abbreviates the refrain as '&c.', supplied here from 10.1. A striking parallel, but for Jainism trees are genuine living beings owed non-harm, not a figure for worthlessness, while the Kural's line is a metaphor.
